entries.title: Rye and caraway
entries.say: As it reads: rye and caraway; tuile, TWEEL.
entries.summary: Rye is the dense, earthy grain of northern Europe and the deli sandwich; caraway is the warm, anise-edged seed most people take for the taste of rye bread. On the fall tartare they meet as a rye tuile and Montreal seasoning.
entries.guest: The rye tuile is a thin, crisp rye wafer for crunch on the tartare, and the Montreal seasoning carries caraway, the seed that flavours rye bread, so the two echo each other.

paras: Rye, Secale cereale, is a hardy cereal that grows where wheat struggles: cold winters, poor sandy soils, short seasons. It became the bread grain of northern and eastern Europe. Its flour is dark, heavy and earthy, faintly sour and a little sweet. The sour, caraway-flecked rye of the Jewish delis of New York and Montreal, the bread under pastrami and smoked meat, is the rye most American guests know.

Caraway, Carum carvi, is the small, curved, ridged seed of a plant in the same family as cumin, fennel, dill and coriander: warm and sharp, with an edge of anise and a bitter finish, and one of the five spices in our Montreal seasoning. Deli rye is nearly always baked with caraway, so most people take the seed's flavour for the grain's. Rye alone is earthy and malty; the anise note is the caraway.

Rye flour behaves nothing like wheat flour. Wheat's proteins join into a stretchy net that traps gas as a dough rises; rye's proteins are there but do not form that net, and rye carries much pentosan, a gummy fibre that soaks up water, so a rye dough is sticky, dense and slack, and a loaf made mostly of rye rises little. Bakers call wheat's net gluten, and rye carries gluten proteins of its own, so a gluten question goes to the service note and the kitchen.

That is why rye bread is made on a sour. Rye's own amylase, the enzyme that turns starch to sugar, stays active in the oven and can leave the crumb gummy; a sourdough's acid checks it and firms the pentosan gel, so the loaf sets. A scald or soaker, whole rye wetted with hot water overnight, tames the coarse meal, and a loaf of mostly rye is baked long and rested a day before cutting, or it gums the knife.

A tuile, say TWEEL, is named for the French roof tile: a thin wafer, baked flat and often curved over a form while warm. A savoury tuile is a paste, not a bread dough, so no rise is needed and rye's weakness does not matter: the easy way to put rye on a plate. A working paste is 100 g (3.5 oz) each of rye flour, soft butter and egg white with a pinch of salt, spread thinly through a stencil and baked at 170°C (338°F) for 6 to 8 minutes until the whole wafer colours.

The deli echo on the fall plate is deliberate. Montreal steak spice belongs to the city's smoked meat delis; that it grew out of the smokehouse's pickling spices is a tale, so tell it as one. Ours is the five the sheet prints: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chilli flake and mustard seed, peppery and aromatic, its heat from the chilli flake; say only those five, whatever a shop blend lists. Beside the tuile, the caraway in the spice meets the rye in the wafer: smoked meat on rye with no bread on it.

A tuile that will not crisp was spread too thick or pulled too early. One that shatters to dust had too little butter or egg white. A limp tuile met damp air; a few minutes in a low oven brings it back once.

Rye began as a weed among the wheat and barley of the Near East and became a crop as farming moved north. Jewish bakers from eastern Europe carried the sour, caraway-seeded loaf to New York and Montreal, where it became the bread of the deli sandwich. Schwartz's, the Montreal smoked meat house, dates from 1928; the tale that the steak spice began over a deli lunch in the 1940s is not verified, so tell it as a tale and give it no date.

At Brennan's rye and caraway meet on one plate, the Steak Tartare with Rye on the Fall 2026 sheet. The rye tuile stands in for the brasserie's toast, crunch against the soft beef and the yolk; the Montreal seasoning is the five the sheet prints. The tuile's recipe and tonight's heat are the chef's answers at lineup. The sheet marks egg, and dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Say tuile as TWEEL and call it a thin, crisp rye wafer, the crunch on the tartare. If a guest says the plate tastes like a deli sandwich, they are right, and the reason is caraway, the seed that carries the flavour they know from rye bread.

faults.fault: A tuile that will not crisp
faults.cause: Spread too thick, or pulled before the whole wafer coloured.
faults.fix: Spread the paste thinly through a stencil and bake until it colours across, not only at the edge.

faults.fault: A tuile that shatters to dust
faults.cause: Too little butter or egg white to bind the rye.
faults.fix: Keep to equal weights of flour, butter and egg white.

faults.cause: It took on moisture from damp air.
faults.fix: A few minutes in a low oven brings it back once; keep the rest in an airtight box.

faults.cause: Toasted too long, or burnt in hot fat.
faults.fix: Toast whole seed in a dry pan for about a minute and lift it out when it smells warm.

faults.fault: A rye dough that spreads like batter
faults.cause: Rye has little stretch; it is sticky by nature.
faults.fix: Use less water and a sourdough rather than more flour, and blend in wheat for a lighter loaf.

The tuile's recipe and tonight's heat are the chef's answers.

cards.front: What is rye, and what does it taste of?
cards.back: A hardy cereal of cold northern Europe, darker and heavier than wheat: earthy, faintly sour and a little sweet, the grain of the deli loaf.

cards.front: What is caraway, and what family does it belong to?
cards.back: The small, curved, ridged seed of a plant in the same family as cumin, fennel, dill and coriander: warm and sharp, with an anise edge and a bitter finish.

cards.front: Which gives rye bread its familiar flavour, the grain or the seed?
cards.back: The seed. Deli rye is nearly always baked with caraway, so people take its anise note for the taste of rye; rye alone is earthy and malty.

cards.front: Why are rye doughs sticky and dense?
cards.back: Rye's proteins do not form the stretchy net wheat's do, and rye carries much pentosan, a gummy fibre that soaks up water, so the dough is slack and the loaf rises little; a sour checks rye's amylase so the crumb sets. Rye is a gluten grain, so a gluten question goes to the service note and the kitchen.

cards.front: What is a tuile, and how do you say it?
cards.back: TWEEL, named for the French roof tile: a thin, crisp wafer baked flat and often curved over a form while warm so it sets in a tile's shape.

cards.front: Why is a tuile the easy way to put rye on a plate?
cards.back: A tuile is a paste, not a bread dough, so it needs no rise; rye's weakness does not matter and its earthy flavour comes through as crunch.

cards.front: What is a working savoury tuile paste, and how is it baked?
cards.back: Equal weights of rye flour, soft butter and egg white with a pinch of salt, spread thinly through a stencil and baked at 170°C (338°F) for 6 to 8 minutes until the whole wafer colours, then shaped at once.

cards.front: What is in our Montreal seasoning?
cards.back: The five the sheet prints: black pepper, caraway, coriander, chilli flake and mustard seed, peppery and aromatic, with its heat from the chilli flake. Say only those five.

cards.front: How do the tuile and the seasoning echo each other on the tartare?
cards.back: The caraway in the Montreal seasoning meets the rye in the tuile, so the plate tastes of the deli's smoked meat on rye with no slice of bread on it.

cards.front: A tuile has gone limp in service. What happened, and what is the fix?
cards.back: It met damp air. A few minutes in a low oven brings it back once; keep the rest in an airtight box, and bake until the whole wafer colours so it crisps fully.

cards.front: What can you say about the Montreal spice's history?
cards.back: It belongs to Montreal's smoked meat delis; Schwartz's dates from 1928. The tale of a deli lunch in the 1940s is not verified, so tell it as a tale with no date.

cards.front: Where do rye and caraway appear on the Brennan's menu?
cards.back: On the Fall 2026 Steak Tartare with Rye, as the rye tuile and the Montreal seasoning. The tuile's recipe and the blend's heat are the chef's answers at lineup.

questions.q: Most guests know the taste of rye bread. Where does that anise-edged flavour come from?
questions.answer: Caraway seed
questions.why: Deli rye is nearly always baked with caraway, so people take the seed's anise note for the grain; rye alone is earthy and malty.

questions.q: Why does a dough made mostly of rye rise so little?
questions.answer: Its proteins form no stretchy net
distractors: Its starch has no sugar for the yeast
Its flour is milled too coarsely to hydrate
It carries too much salt for the yeast
questions.why: Wheat's proteins join into a net that traps gas; rye's do not, and much gummy pentosan makes the dough slack, so the loaf stays close. Rye is a gluten grain: a gluten question goes to the service note and the kitchen.

questions.q: Why is a loaf of mostly rye made on a sour rather than on yeast alone?
questions.answer: The acid checks rye's amylase so the crumb sets
distractors: The acid makes the dough stretch like wheat
Rye flour cannot feed baker's yeast
The sour bleaches the dark crumb paler
questions.why: Rye's own amylase keeps turning starch to sugar in the oven and leaves a gummy crumb; a sourdough's acid checks it and firms the pentosan gel, which is also why the loaf rests a day before cutting.

questions.q: What is a tuile named for?
questions.answer: The French roof tile
questions.why: Tuile is French for a roof tile: the wafer is baked flat and often draped over a form while warm so it sets in a tile's curve.

questions.q: Why does the kitchen put rye on the plate as a tuile rather than as a bread?
questions.answer: A tuile needs no rise, so rye's weakness does not matter
distractors: Rye bread cannot be sliced thin enough
A tuile keeps for months at room temperature
Rye flour cannot be baked above 150°C (302°F)
questions.why: A tuile is a paste, not a dough; nothing has to rise, so the flour's lack of stretch costs nothing and its earthy flavour comes through as crunch.

questions.q: Which five spices make up our Montreal seasoning?
questions.answer: Black pepper, caraway, coriander, chilli flake, mustard seed
distractors: Fennel, star anise, cinnamon, ginger, white pepper
questions.why: Those are the five the sheet prints; a shop blend may add garlic, dill or salt, so name only ours and send the question of heat to the chef.

questions.q: What does the caraway in the seasoning do against the rye tuile?
questions.answer: It echoes the rye, like the deli's bread
distractors: It cools the heat of the chilli flake
It cures the raw beef as it sits
questions.why: Caraway is the seed that flavours deli rye, so the spice and the wafer together taste of smoked meat on rye without a slice of bread.

questions.q: A rye tuile has gone soft during service. What is the likeliest cause?
questions.answer: It took on moisture from the air
distractors: The paste had too much salt
It was shaped while still warm
questions.why: A thin wafer draws water from damp air and loses its snap; a few minutes in a low oven dries it once, and an airtight box keeps the rest crisp.

questions.q: A guest asks when Montreal steak spice was invented. What is the honest answer?
questions.answer: No date: the deli lunch tale is unverified
distractors: It was created at Schwartz's in 1928
It was first blended in Toronto in 1950
questions.why: Schwartz's dates from 1928, but the story that the spice began over a lunch in the 1940s is unverified; tell it as a tale and give it no date.

entries.title: Fresh pasta and agnolotti
entries.say: As it reads: fresh pasta; agnolotti del plin, ah-nyoh-LOT-tee del PLEEN.
entries.summary: Fresh egg pasta is soft wheat flour and egg rolled thin and cooked in a minute or two; dried pasta is durum semolina and water, extruded and dried to a firm bite. The menu carries both: pinched agnolotti, rough frascarelli, shells and buttered noodles.
entries.guest: Agnolotti del plin are small pinched pasta parcels from Piedmont, plin being the pinch that seals them. Ours come with pork, braised collards, ricotta, Parmesan and crisp lemon breadcrumbs.

paras: Pasta is a dough of milled wheat and liquid, shaped and boiled. Fresh egg pasta is soft wheat flour, the fine Italian 00 grade, worked with whole eggs into a firm dough, rested, rolled thin and cut or filled. It cooks in one to three minutes and eats tender and rich.

Dried pasta is durum semolina and water. Durum is the hardest wheat; its coarse yellow semolina makes a stiff dough that is forced through a die, extruded, into shells, tubes and strands and dried slowly. Italian law has reserved dried pasta for durum semolina since 1967, and the decree of 2001 that now governs it defines pasta di semola di grano duro as semolina and water. It holds a firm bite, al dente, to the tooth, and its shape was made to carry sauce.

The master ratio is 100 g (3.5 oz) of 00 flour to one large egg, about 50 g (1.75 oz), with a pinch of salt. Make a well in the flour, beat the eggs in the centre and draw the flour in, then knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and springy. Rest it, wrapped, for at least 30 minutes, then roll it thin enough to read print through.

For agnolotti del plin, say ah-nyoh-LOT-tee del PLEEN, pipe small knobs of filling along the edge of a sheet, fold the edge over them, press out the air, then pinch the dough shut between each knob with thumb and finger: that pinch is the plin, the Piedmont dialect word that names them. Frascarelli, say frah-skah-REL-lee, are flour wetted with beaten egg, or with water in the Marche tradition, stirred so it gathers into rough, irregular lumps, sieved of loose flour and boiled.

Use a big pot, 1 litre (about 1 quart) of water with 10 g (2 tsp) of salt for every 100 g (3.5 oz) of pasta, at a rolling boil. Pull the pasta a minute before it is done, keep a cup of the cloudy water and finish it in the pan with its sauce: the starch in that water joins the fat into a sauce that clings, and the oldest sauce of all is butter and grated cheese melted into it. Never rinse: that washes the starch away.

Fresh egg pasta is cut into tagliatelle and pappardelle, filled as ravioli and pinched as plin. Dried durum pasta runs from spaghetti to conchiglie, say kon-KEEL-yeh, the ridged shells pressed through a shaped die: every curve holds sauce, which is why the Shells & Cheese takes them.

Parcels that burst in the water held air or were not pinched hard enough; the air expands and splits the seam. Pasta that sticks in a clump went into too little water or was not stirred at the start. Sauce that pools under the pasta was poured over drained pasta; finish it in the pan with a splash of the water.

The tale that Marco Polo brought pasta from China has no foundation: a twelfth-century Arab geographer described dried pasta being made near Palermo. Agnolotti del plin are the pasta of the Langhe, the hills around Alba in Piedmont. Frascarelli belong to the Marche, where the flour-and-water version is the tradition.

At Brennan's the pack carries pasta on four plates. The Agnolotti del Plin on the Fall 2026 sheet are plated with pork, braised collards, ricotta and Parmesan and finished with lemon pangrattato; the sheet does not say which parts sit inside the parcels and which around them, so learn the build at lineup. The Chateau Espagnole's frascarelli are flour and egg loosely combined into irregular pieces, boiled and finished in butter.

The Shells & Cheese folds dried shells into a Mimolette and Abita Amber fondue, and the children's Buttered Noodles with Cheese are tossed with butter and cheese; the card names neither shape nor cheese. Pasta is wheat, so dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Say agnolotti del plin and tell the pinch: a thin sheet folded over small fillings and pinched shut between them. Call the frascarelli small, rustic pasta pieces finished in butter. What goes into tonight's dough is the kitchen's answer.

faults.fault: Dough that tears on the roller
faults.fix: Work in a splash of water and rest it for 30 minutes under a cloth before rolling again.

faults.fault: Parcels that burst in the water
faults.cause: Air left inside, or a pinch that was not firm.
faults.fix: Press the air out as you fold and pinch hard between the fillings before cutting.

faults.cause: Too little water, or no stir at the start.
faults.fix: A big pot at a rolling boil, stirred as the pasta goes in.

faults.cause: Drained pasta dressed on the plate.
faults.fix: Finish it in the pan with a splash of the starchy water so the sauce clings.
Pull it a minute early; it keeps cooking in the sauce.

brennans.how: Thin sheets folded over small fillings and pinched shut, plin being the pinch, then cut apart. The sheet lists pork, braised collards, ricotta, Parmesan and lemon pangrattato without saying which sit inside the parcels and which around them, so learn the build at lineup.

Small, rustic pasta pieces with roots in the Marche: the sheet describes flour and egg loosely combined into irregular pieces, boiled and finished in butter, the soft comfort beside the lean beef and the Espagnole. The egg and the butter are this house's treatment, not the Marche rule.

Conchiglie, dried durum shells, boiled in well salted water to al dente, drained and never rinsed so the starch helps the Mimolette and Abita Amber fondue cling in every curve. Whether the shells are cooked to order or held is the kitchen's method.

Noodles boiled in salted water until just tender, drained and tossed at once with butter, grated cheese and a splash of the pasta water so the cheese melts into a light gloss. The card names neither the shape nor the cheese, so a parent's question goes to the kitchen.

cards.front: What is the difference between fresh egg pasta and dried pasta?
cards.back: Fresh is soft wheat flour and egg, rolled thin and cooked in a minute or two, tender and rich. Dried is durum semolina and water, extruded and dried, firm and made to hold its shape.

cards.front: What is the master ratio for fresh egg pasta?
cards.back: 100 g (3.5 oz) of 00 flour to one large egg, about 50 g (1.75 oz), with a pinch of salt; knead until springy and rest for at least 30 minutes.

cards.front: What are agnolotti del plin, and what does plin mean?
cards.back: Piedmont's small filled pasta: a thin sheet folded over knobs of filling and pinched shut between each one. Plin is the dialect word for that pinch; the parcels are cut apart along it.

cards.front: What are frascarelli, and where are they from?
cards.back: Rough pasta pieces of the Marche: flour wetted with egg, or with water in the tradition there, stirred into irregular lumps, sieved of loose flour, boiled and finished in butter.

cards.front: How much water and salt does pasta need?
cards.back: A big pot: 1 litre (about 1 quart) of water with 10 g (2 tsp) of salt for every 100 g (3.5 oz) of pasta, at a rolling boil, stirred at the start.

cards.front: Why pull pasta a minute early and finish it in the pan?
cards.back: It keeps cooking in the sauce, and a splash of the starchy water joins the fat into a sauce that clings to every piece instead of pooling beneath it.

cards.front: Why is pasta never rinsed after draining?
cards.back: Rinsing washes away the surface starch that helps a sauce cling, so the sauce slides off; drain it, keep some of the water, and dress it at once.

cards.front: Why does the Shells & Cheese use conchiglie?
cards.back: Conchiglie, kon-KEEL-yeh, are dried durum shells, ridged outside and hollow within, made to hold sauce in every curve; here the Mimolette and Abita Amber fondue.

cards.front: What does Italian law say dried durum pasta may be made from?
cards.back: Durum wheat semolina and water alone: the rule dates from the law of 1967, and the decree of 2001 that now governs it defines pasta di semola di grano duro the same way; egg pasta and special pastas are defined separately.

cards.front: Filled parcels burst in the water. What went wrong?
cards.back: Air was left inside, or the pinch was not firm: trapped air expands in the boil and splits the seam. Press the air out and pinch hard before cutting.

cards.front: Which Brennan's plates carry pasta, and what should you learn at lineup?
cards.back: The Agnolotti del Plin, the frascarelli on the Chateau Espagnole, the Shells & Cheese and the children's buttered noodles. The agnolotti's build and the frascarelli's batch are lineup questions.

cards.front: Did Marco Polo bring pasta from China?
cards.back: No: the tale has no foundation. A twelfth-century Arab geographer described dried pasta made near Palermo, and fresh egg pasta belongs to the Po valley.

questions.q: Which wheat and liquid make classic dried pasta?
questions.answer: Durum semolina and water
questions.why: Durum is the hardest wheat; its semolina makes a stiff dough that is extruded and dried and holds a firm bite. Fresh pasta is the soft flour and egg.

questions.q: What is the master ratio for fresh egg pasta?
questions.answer: 100 g (3.5 oz) of flour to one large egg
distractors: 500 g (1 lb) of flour to one large egg
100 g (3.5 oz) of flour to six large eggs
Equal weights of flour and water, no egg
questions.why: One egg, about 50 g (1.75 oz), hydrates 100 g (3.5 oz) of 00 flour into a firm, springy dough; richer doughs swap some whole eggs for yolks.

questions.q: What does plin mean in agnolotti del plin?
questions.answer: The pinch that seals each parcel
distractors: The roast juices they are dressed with
questions.why: Plin is the Piedmont dialect word for a pinch: the sheet is folded over the fillings and pinched shut between them, then cut apart along the pinches.

questions.q: How much salt goes into 1 litre (about 1 quart) of pasta water?
questions.answer: About 10 g (2 tsp)
distractors: A pinch, so the sauce can be seasoned
questions.why: Ten grams a litre seasons the pasta itself as it cooks; a pinch leaves it flat and a heavy hand makes it inedible. Salt does not toughen pasta.

questions.q: Why keep a cup of the pasta water before draining?
questions.answer: Its starch binds the sauce to the pasta
distractors: It cools the pasta before plating
It is used to rinse the pasta
It replaces salt in the sauce
questions.why: The cloudy water carries starch; tossed with the pasta and its fat over heat, it turns the sauce glossy and makes it cling instead of pooling.

questions.q: Why are shells the shape for the Shells & Cheese?
questions.answer: Their ridges and hollows hold sauce
distractors: They cook faster than any other shape
They are made from fresh egg dough
questions.why: Conchiglie are ridged outside and hollow within, pressed through a die to carry sauce in every curve, here a Mimolette and Abita Amber fondue.

questions.q: Agnolotti burst in the boil. What is the likeliest cause?
questions.answer: Air was trapped inside the parcel
distractors: The water was salted too heavily
The water was at a bare simmer
questions.why: Trapped air expands in boiling water and splits the seam; press the air out as you fold and pinch firmly between the fillings before cutting.

questions.q: Under Italian law, what may classic dried pasta be made from?
questions.answer: Durum semolina and water only
distractors: Semolina with up to half soft flour
questions.why: The 1967 law reserved dried pasta for durum semolina, and the 2001 decree that updated it defines pasta di semola di grano duro as semolina and water; egg pasta and special pastas are their own categories, and soft wheat is kept out.

entries.title: Dark chocolate
entries.say: As it reads: dark chocolate; cremeux, kray-MUH.
entries.summary: Chocolate is roasted cocoa bean ground to a paste, with cocoa butter and sugar added; a bar's percentage is the share that came from the bean. That share sets dark, bittersweet, milk and white, and the pastry kitchen melts, sets and tempers it.
entries.guest: The chocolate crémeux is a smooth, dense chocolate cream, with bitter cocoa nibs for crunch, lemon olive oil and flakes of sea salt that make the chocolate taste more of itself.

paras: Chocolate begins as the seeds of Theobroma cacao. The beans are scooped from the pod with their pulp and fermented for several days, then dried, roasted, cracked and winnowed so the shell blows away and the broken kernel, the nib, remains. Ground, the nibs flow into a dark paste, chocolate liquor or cocoa mass: about half cocoa butter, the fat, and half cocoa solids, the flavour. A bar is that liquor with sugar and usually extra cocoa butter, conched, stirred for hours until smooth.
The percentage on the wrapper is the share of the bar that came from the bean, butter and solids together: a 70 per cent bar is about 30 per cent sugar.

The kinds are set by that share. In the United States a bar sold as bittersweet or semisweet must hold at least 35 per cent chocolate liquor, and pastry cooks usually mean 60 to 72 per cent cocoa by dark. Milk chocolate holds at least 10 per cent liquor and 12 per cent milk solids, and dairy questions about it go to the service note and the kitchen. White chocolate is cocoa butter, sugar and milk solids with no cocoa solids at all. Cocoa nibs are the roasted bean broken into bitter, crunchy pieces, chocolate before anything is added: not chocolate chips.

Chocolate melts gently: chop it fine and warm it over barely simmering water, stirring, never above about 50°C (122°F) for dark; cocoa butter melts at about 34°C (93°F). A single drop of water seizes melting chocolate, the sugar and solids clumping into a stiff, grainy mass, and the cure is more liquid, not less: whisk in warm cream and use it as a sauce. A ganache is chocolate and hot cream blended to a glossy emulsion, equal weights for a dark chocolate that sets soft.

A crémeux, say kray-MUH, is a crème anglaise, the stirred custard, poured hot over chopped chocolate, blended smooth and chilled, so the chocolate's own cocoa butter firms it as it cools: denser than a mousse, softer than a ganache, nothing whipped in. Tempering, for shine and snap, is the discipline of cocoa butter: melt dark chocolate to 45 to 50°C (113 to 122°F), cool it to 27 to 28°C (81 to 82°F) while stirring so stable crystals form, then rework it to 31 to 32°C (88 to 90°F) to use.

Seized chocolate met a drop of water: whisk in warm liquid and make a sauce. Scorched chocolate, lumpy and smelling burnt, was heated too hard; there is no rescue. Grey streaks or a dull, soft bar are fat bloom, cocoa butter set in the wrong crystal by bad tempering or warm storage; the chocolate is sound and can be tempered again.

Cacao is a tree of the Americas. The oldest trace of its use, about 5,300 years old, was found on pottery in the Ecuadorian Amazon. The smooth bar is a nineteenth-century invention: conching, the long stirring that makes chocolate smooth, was worked out by Rodolphe Lindt in Bern in 1879.

At Brennan's the pack carries chocolate on three plates. The Fall 2026 Chocolate Crémeux is a crème anglaise set with chocolate, marked with gelatine on the sheet, under a cocoa nib crumble, a lemon olive oil and Maldon salt; the sheet names the chocolate only as chocolate, so promise neither dark nor milk. The Café Brûlot Coffee Cake bakes bittersweet chocolate with chicory coffee. The Snickers' Bavarian milk chocolate is read as milk chocolate in a Bavarian cream, not chocolate from Bavaria. No maker, origin or percentage is printed for any of them: those are lineup questions, and dairy questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

Describe the crémeux as a smooth, dense chocolate cream with crunchy bitter nibs, bright lemon oil and crisp salt that makes the chocolate taste more of itself. The Banyuls, the sweet fortified red, is the glass the dinner tasting pours with chocolate; à la carte, and with the coffee cake at breakfast, offer it only once the sommelier confirms it is poured by the glass and at what price, and our chicory coffee is the other partner. A question about milk, eggs or gelatine in a chocolate dish goes to the kitchen.

brennans.how: A crème anglaise poured hot over chopped chocolate, blended to a glossy emulsion and chilled, the cocoa butter firming the set, with gelatine marked on the sheet. The nib crumble is the crunch and the bitter edge. The sheet names no maker, origin or percentage: ask at lineup.

Bittersweet chocolate baked with chicory coffee, which deepens it, since coffee and chocolate share roasted, bitter notes. No maker is printed, so the bar is the chef's answer, and dietary questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

The Bavarian milk chocolate is read as milk chocolate in a Bavarian cream, not chocolate from Bavaria: sweeter and softer, with milk solids. The guide flags peanuts in capitals, so confirm before ordering for every table, and send any nut question to the kitchen.

cards.front: How does a cocoa bean become chocolate?
cards.back: Fermented, dried and roasted, cracked and winnowed to nibs, then ground to chocolate liquor; sugar and extra cocoa butter are added, and the mass is refined and conched smooth.

cards.front: What does the percentage on a bar describe?
cards.back: The share of the bar that came from the bean, cocoa butter and cocoa solids together; the rest is mostly sugar. A 70 per cent bar is about 30 per cent sugar.

cards.front: What sets dark, bittersweet, milk and white chocolate apart?
cards.back: The share of chocolate liquor: bittersweet at least 35 per cent by the US rule, usually 60 to 72 per cent; milk chocolate adds milk solids; white chocolate has no cocoa solids at all.

cards.front: What are cocoa nibs?
cards.back: The roasted bean broken into bitter, crunchy pieces with the shell winnowed away: chocolate before any sugar is added. Not chocolate chips.

cards.front: What happens when a drop of water meets melting chocolate, and what is the fix?
cards.back: It seizes: sugar and solids clump into a stiff, grainy mass. The fix is more liquid, not less: whisk in warm cream and use it as a sauce.

cards.front: What is a crémeux, and how do you say it?
cards.back: kray-MUH, French for creamy: a crème anglaise poured hot over chocolate, blended and chilled so the cocoa butter sets it. Denser than a mousse, softer than a ganache, nothing whipped in.

cards.front: What are the tempering temperatures for dark chocolate?
cards.back: Melt to 45 to 50°C (113 to 122°F), cool to 27 to 28°C (81 to 82°F) while stirring, then rework to 31 to 32°C (88 to 90°F) to use. The reward is shine and snap.

cards.front: What are the grey streaks on an old bar?
cards.back: Fat bloom: cocoa butter that set in the wrong crystal from poor tempering or warm storage. The chocolate is sound; melt and temper it again. A gritty pale dusting is sugar bloom from damp.

cards.front: What is a ganache, and what is the dark chocolate ratio?
cards.back: Chocolate and hot cream blended to a glossy emulsion; equal weights give a dark chocolate ganache that sets soft, and more cream makes a sauce.

cards.front: Where does chocolate appear on the Brennan's menu?
cards.back: The Fall 2026 Chocolate Crémeux with cocoa nib crumble, lemon olive oil and Maldon salt; the bittersweet chocolate of the Café Brûlot Coffee Cake; the Bavarian milk chocolate of The Snickers.

cards.front: A guest asks which chocolate is in the crémeux. What do you say?
cards.back: The sheet names it only as chocolate, with no maker, origin or percentage, so promise neither dark nor milk and ask the chef; dairy questions go to the service note and the kitchen.

cards.front: How old is the use of cacao, and when did chocolate become smooth?
cards.back: The oldest trace, about 5,300 years old, is on pottery from the Ecuadorian Amazon. Conching, the long stirring that makes chocolate smooth, was worked out by Rodolphe Lindt in Bern in 1879.

questions.q: A bar is marked 70 per cent. What does the figure describe?
questions.answer: The share that came from the cocoa bean
distractors: The share that is cocoa butter alone
How bitter it will taste, out of 100
questions.why: The percentage counts cocoa butter and cocoa solids together, everything from the bean; the rest is mostly sugar, so a 70 per cent bar is about 30 per cent sugar.

questions.q: Under the US rule, what is the least chocolate liquor a bittersweet bar may hold?
questions.answer: 35 per cent
questions.why: Bittersweet and semisweet share the 35 per cent floor; pastry cooks usually reach for 60 to 72 per cent, and milk chocolate's floor is 10 per cent liquor.

questions.q: A guest hears cocoa nibs and pictures chocolate chips. What are nibs?
questions.answer: Roasted cocoa bean broken into bitter pieces
distractors: Small drops of tempered dark chocolate
questions.why: Nibs are the cracked, winnowed kernel of the roasted bean before any sugar is added: crunchy, bitter and a little fruity, chocolate before chocolate.

questions.q: A drop of water fell into melting chocolate and it turned stiff and grainy. What now?
questions.answer: Whisk in warm cream and use it as a sauce
distractors: Heat it harder until it loosens
questions.why: Seized chocolate needs more liquid, not less: enough warm cream dissolves the clumps into a smooth sauce, while more heat scorches it.

questions.q: What sets a chocolate crémeux as it chills?
questions.answer: The chocolate's own cocoa butter
distractors: A thick layer of whipped cream
questions.why: The hot custard melts the chocolate; as the cream cools its cocoa butter firms, giving the dense, glossy set. Some kitchens add a little gelatine for a firmer one.

questions.q: To what temperature is tempered dark chocolate reworked for use?
questions.why: Melting goes to 45 to 50°C (113 to 122°F) and cooling to 27 to 28°C (81 to 82°F); the working window of 31 to 32°C (88 to 90°F) keeps only the stable crystals.

questions.q: An old bar shows grey streaks and a dull surface. What is it?
questions.answer: Fat bloom from cocoa butter out of temper
questions.why: Fat bloom is cocoa butter that set in the wrong crystal after poor tempering or warm storage; the bar is sound and can be melted and tempered again.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the crémeux is dark or milk chocolate. What is the honest answer?
questions.answer: Ask the chef; the sheet names only chocolate
distractors: Dark, since every crémeux is dark
White, to take the lemon oil
questions.why: The sheet prints no maker, origin or percentage, so promise neither dark nor milk; the kitchen says which bar it is, and dairy questions go to the service note.
